1.explanation: All of the core logic for XML tag name detection lives inside the default export in xml.js. The constant TAG_NAME_RE defines what constitutes a valid tag name (including an optional namespace prefix), and both the open-tag and close-tag rules wrap lookaheads around TAG_NAME_RE to decide whether a '<…>' sequence is a tag. Because the optional namespace sub-pattern is written as /[A-Z0-9_.-]+:/ (one or more characters from A–Z, 0–9, underscore, period or hyphen, followed by a colon), it never matches a single alphabetical character plus ':' (e.g. “a:”). As a result, TAG_NAME_RE simply fails to match those tags, and highlight.js does not apply the tag styling. Fixing the issue requires adjusting the TAG_NAME_RE (and thereby the open/close tag modes) to allow single-character prefixes before the colon.
1.bug_scenario: In the provided screenshots you can see that XML tags with multi‐character namespace prefixes (e.g. <abc:OK>, <ab:OK>) are correctly syntax-highlighted, but a single-letter prefix (<a:FAIL>) is not highlighted at all. In other words, the TAG_NAME_RE regex in the XML language definition fails to match “a:” as a namespace prefix, so any tag whose prefix is only one character stops being recognized as a tag name and loses its highlighting.

2.explanation: All of the tag‐matching logic for XML lives in the default export in src/languages/xml.js. In particular it defines TAG_NAME_RE and then uses it in the open‐ and close‐tag grammar entries (begin patterns). Because TAG_NAME_RE is built with regex.optional(/[A-Z0-9_.-]+:/) (one or more characters before the colon), it fails to match a single‐character namespace prefix. Thus the default export’s grammar rules do not recognize “a:Tag” as a valid tag name, causing those elements to go unhighlighted.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting XML with namespace prefixes, tags with multi‐character prefixes (e.g. “abc:OK”, “ab:OK”) are correctly recognized and colored, but tags whose namespace prefixes are a single letter (e.g. “a:OK”) are not matched by the grammar and therefore not highlighted. The screenshots show that <a:FAIL xmlns:a="…" /> appears in plain text, while other namespace‐prefixed tags remain highlighted.
